Transformers Model Integration Contracts

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1284 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that on July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5.
  • It has been revealed that when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them.
  • Recent findings suggest that transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that on July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

It has been revealed that when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Recent findings suggest that transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Sources indicate that model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:.

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

It has been revealed that A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

Recent findings suggest that for example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:.

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

It has been revealed that A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

It has been revealed that the Llama 4 Scout shrink report highlights what this looks like on a massive model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:.

Recent findings suggest that it drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

Sources indicate that we used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:.

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

Recent findings suggest that as of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:.

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

General Mitigation Factors Recommended security practices and firewall configurations can help protect an industrial control system network from attacks that originate from outside the network. Such practices include that process control systems are physically protected from direct access by unauthorized personnel, have no direct connections to the Internet, and are separated from other networks by means of a firewall system that has a minimal number of ports exposed, and others that have to be evaluated case by case. Industrial control systems should not be used for Internet surfing, instant messaging, or receiving e-mails. Portable computers and removable storage media should be carefully scanned for viruses before they are connected to a control system. Additional information on Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity Best Practices can be found in the Hitachi Energy’s “Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity Best Practices” Cybersecurity Notification. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. Michael Prebil is a Cybersecurity Workforce Analyst for NICE at NIST, supporting the development, improvement, and implementation of the NICE Workforce Framework for Cybersecurity (NICE Framework).

It has been revealed that previously, he was a senior policy analyst at New America’s Center on Education & Labor, where he focused on issues related to apprenticeship, community colleges, and job quality. In that role, Michael studied credentialing and work-based learning programs and policies, and provided technical assistance for states and cities implementing career pathways across a variety of fields, including cybersecurity and IT.

Recent findings suggest that michael received his undergraduate degree in history from McGill University, and a graduate certificate from the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies. He has also studied at the Community College of Baltimore County and is currently pursuing a graduate degree in statistics at the City University of New York’s Hunter College.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, with retrieval instructions in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, you can customize answers per tenant.
  • It has been revealed that now you write that guidance once, as a managed, versioned Amazon Bedrock resource, and each request references it.
  • Industry observers note that take AnyCompany Smart Home, a fictitious firm that sells a home controller and room sensors in three sales regions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, with retrieval instructions in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, you can customize answers per tenant. The same product and policy documents often serve several audiences, such as customers in different regions or internal teams, and each audience needs its own answer. You set the voice, format, retrieval guidance, and answer policy that agentic retrieval applies to each request. Before this feature, you couldn’t set the answer style, so agentic retrieval could use a different style from one request to the next. For a fixed voice or structured output, you had to turn off response generation, call a model yourself, and maintain the prompt in every application.

It has been revealed that now you write that guidance once, as a managed, versioned Amazon Bedrock resource, and each request references it. When you change an instruction, you can pin a version so that each application switches to the fresh version when you’re ready.

Industry observers note that take AnyCompany Smart Home, a fictitious firm that sells a home controller and room sensors in three sales regions. Its customer assistant serves all three regions, and its support, field sales, and legal teams use internal assistants that they built on the same documents. AnyCompany defines each region and internal team as a tenant here, and each needs a different answer. A customer in Sales Region Central needs Spanish with day/month/year dates, and a support agent needs a short ticket note. To keep the example compact, every tenant queries one knowledge base. However, agentic retrieval can search up to five knowledge bases in a single request, and the tenant’s instruction applies to all of them.

Retrieval instructions change how the assistant answers, but they aren’t an authorization or data-isolation boundary. Use metadata filters or separate knowledge bases to control what each tenant can retrieve. In this post, we show how to give each tenant its own answers from shared knowledge bases while keeping each tenant’s data separate. By the end, you can roll out a change to one tenant’s instruction and confirm which version answered each request.

Industry observers note that tenants that share documents still differ in language, date and money conventions, voice, and which policy values they can quote. A retrieval instruction has four fields for these differences:.

Sources indicate that the persona, answerFormat, and answerPolicy fields apply only when generateResponse is true, which is the default, and retrievalGuidance applies either way. For details, see Create and manage retrieval instructions. Table 1 indicates how the answer to the same return question changes when the request includes the Sales Region Central instruction and names the customer’s region.

Table 1: The same return question with and without the Sales Region Central instruction.

These patterns come up across industries. An enterprise software provider can run one assistant for many of its own customers. Each customer uploads its policies, standard operating procedures, and firm values, and persona and answerPolicy give each one its own voice and rules. A regulated enterprise can put a fixed disclaimer in answerPolicy and a set citation form in answerFormat, so every answer includes both. A team that sends answers to downstream code can get strict JSON from an answerFormat, without a separate generation step. In each case, the documents are shared, and the voice, format, and policy change from caller to caller.

An instruction belongs to your AWS account and AWS Region, not to a knowledge base, and goes through these stages:.

In a recent development, instructions set voice, format, conventions, and policy wording. They don’t limit which documents the agent can retrieve, and they don’t choose the tenant’s own values, which come from naming the tenant in the request. Use metadata filters or separate knowledge bases to limit what each tenant can retrieve.

Each tenant gets its own instruction and metadata filter. The instruction sets the voice, format, and policy of the answer, and the filter limits which documents the agent retrieves. Your backend chooses both from the authenticated tenant, so one shared knowledge base can serve every tenant. In Figure 1, your backend maps the authenticated tenant to an instruction version and a metadata filter, and adds a short tenant line to the message. Then it calls AgenticRetrieveStream on one shared managed knowledge base.

Figure 1: One managed knowledge base with per-tenant instructions and filters.

According to recent reports, the same pattern works with a separate knowledge base for each tenant. A request can query a shared global knowledge base and the tenant’s own knowledge base together, each with its own filter.

According to recent reports, the example uses 32 short, fictitious AnyCompany Smart Home policy and product documents for the AnySmartProduct-5 home controller and AnySmartProduct-6 room sensors. They’re stored in an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket, and each has region, audience_team, and sensitivity metadata. Each of the six tenants, three regions and three teams, has its own instruction pinned to version 1. Two restricted engineering notes belong to no tenant, so no tenant’s filter should return them.

Industry observers note that the code is in the GitHub repo, in Python and TypeScript, and runs in the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1) by default. To use another AWS Region, set AWS_REGION. For the latest Region support, see Supported AWS Regions.

According to recent reports, examples use Python with these two clients. Later snippets leave out the client setup and import lines.

The Sales Region Central instruction sets the language, date and money formats, and policy wording:.

To create and pin each tenant’s instruction:.

According to recent reports, this code runs steps 3 and 6. The repo version adds the polling for steps 4 and 5.

An update replaces the whole instruction, including the description, so resend every field you want to keep. To encrypt an instruction with your own key, set customerEncryptionKeyArn when you create it. You can’t add or change the key later. Your key policy also needs the statement in Encryption of retrieval instructions.

Industry observers note that an instruction doesn’t limit which documents the agent retrieves. On a shared knowledge base, a Sales Region North customer’s question can return the Sales Region Central and South addenda, and even notes that no tenant should see. To keep each tenant to its own documents, add a metadata filter built from the authenticated tenant, or give the tenant its own knowledge base. A request can still query the tenant’s knowledge base alongside shared ones. Figure 2 compares the three approaches.

Figure 2: Where tenant isolation comes from.

In a recent development, A metadata filter keeps one knowledge base to sync and maintain, but every document needs accurate metadata, and your backend must build the filter correctly on every request. A separate knowledge base per tenant isolates tenant data by design, but each tenant adds a knowledge base and data source to create, sync, and pay for. You can combine them: one request can query a shared knowledge base and the tenant’s own knowledge base, each with its own filter.

With a tenant filter or a separate knowledge base, the agent retrieves only documents the tenant is entitled to, so answers don’t quote other regions’ values. An answer policy that limits the assistant to one region helps, but without a filter an answer can still quote another region’s value.

Build the filter on your server from the authenticated tenant, because Amazon Bedrock applies whatever filter the request sends:.

This filter uses the equals, andAll, and orAll operators on document metadata. It isn’t per-user access filtering through userContext.

Recent findings suggest that answer policies are best effort. A line such as “Never share restricted engineering notes” can keep values out of the answer. If the notes are retrieved, though, an answer can still name the mechanism or record ID. To keep restricted content out of answers, exclude it with a metadata filter.

According to recent reports, for each request, your backend sends the tenant’s instruction ID and version, the tenant filter, and a tenant line. A tenant line is a short sentence, such as Customer sales region: Sales Region Central., placed before the question:.

Here’s the same return question answered with three tenant instructions on one knowledge base, trimmed:.

Recent findings suggest that A tenant line tells the agent who is asking, which helps the answer quote that tenant’s values. It doesn’t set the tenant’s language, answer format, or date and money formats, so pair it with the tenant’s instruction. Without the instruction, a Sales Region Central answer can come back in English, without the Source: line, or in the wrong date format.

Without an instruction, a customer answer can also quote internal discount tiers from a document the tenant can retrieve. An answer policy that forbids them, like the Sales Region Central one, can keep them out, but to make sure, filter out the document that contains them. Team formats such as the ticket note aren’t guaranteed on every answer, so validate the format in any code that depends on it.

Instructions change how an answer is written. The facts still come from the documents the agent retrieves, so compute exact values such as a return deadline in your application.

According to recent reports, A request can reference only one retrieval instruction. When a user belongs to both a region and a team, that instruction has to cover both. For example, a support agent in Sales Region South needs the support team’s voice and the region’s date and money formats. Table 2 compares two ways to set that up for N regions and M teams.

Table 2: Two ways to cover a region and a team with one instruction.

Industry observers note that start with the team’s instruction and a region tenant line, which keeps the count at N + M. Add a combined instruction only for pairs whose formats differ from the team’s default. Neither approach limits what the agent retrieves, so keep the tenant filter on every request. A filter also can’t remove a value from a shared document the tenant is entitled to, such as a global policy that lists every region’s dates. As of this writing, the default quota is 50 retrieval instructions per account per AWS Region, and you can request an increase. Combined instructions add up promptly, with 15 for 3 regions and 3 teams and 65 for 10 regions and 5 teams.

In a recent development, if your application calls agentic retrieval with the same role for every tenant, IAM can’t tell tenants apart, and your code alone chooses each request’s instruction and filter. When each tenant’s requests run under that tenant’s own credentials, tag conditions add a second check on which instruction a request can apply and who can change it. Those credentials can come from a role per tenant or a role assumed with a tenant session tag.

AgenticRetrieveStream has no IAM resource. To apply an instruction, the caller needs bedrock:GetRetrievalInstruction on the instruction’s Amazon Resource Name (ARN), so that’s where the tag condition goes. These attribute-based access control (ABAC) statements from the example’s AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) app scope one tenant:.

Sources indicate that with these statements, a tenant’s applier role can apply only instructions tagged with its tenant, and its tenant admin role can manage only those instructions. The platform admin can manage any tenant’s instructions. Require both tag conditions on TagResource. With only the request-tag condition, a tenant admin can retag another tenant’s instruction into its own scope. To add a tenant, add its key to the tenantRoles context value and deploy the AWS CDK app again with the same trustedPrincipalArn. Apply permission doesn’t limit retrieval, so scope bedrock:Retrieve to each role’s knowledge bases. ListRetrievalInstructions can’t be scoped by tag, so keep instruction names free of sensitive information.

Sources indicate that as Use retrieval instructions with agentic retrieval describes, the first Planning trace event includes appliedInstruction, with the ID and version of the instruction that was applied. Log it with the tenant ID:.

For every event type, see the AgenticRetrieveStream API reference. To capture the applied instruction, check for the first Planning event in the loop that reads the answer:.

For an audit record outside your application, use AWS CloudTrail. CloudTrail logs Agents for Amazon Bedrock Runtime operations, including AgenticRetrieveStream, as data events. A trail records data events only after you enable them. For details, see Monitor Amazon Bedrock API calls using CloudTrail.

Amazon Bedrock doesn’t route traffic between versions. Keep a release configuration for each tenant, pin its version on every request, and canary, promote, or roll back by changing that pin. The trace confirms which version served each request, not whether the upcoming version answers better, so gate each promotion on your own checks. This release configuration is from the repo’s router:.

Recent findings suggest that to change one tenant, update its instruction, wait for the review, create a version, and move only that tenant’s pin. For example, moving the support tenant to version 2 leaves the other five tenants on version 1:.

A pin fixes the instruction, not the exact wording of each answer. During an update review, DRAFT keeps serving the previous content. A version create or a second update during the review fails with HTTP 409, so poll until the review finishes, as the retrieval instruction rollout steps describe.

In a recent development, retrieval instructions aren’t only for multi-tenant setups. The same fields work for a single application, such as an assistant that has to return JSON for downstream code or keep one voice across every answer. The repo has code for the first three.

An answerFormat can replace your own generation step:.

In a recent development, with this answerFormat, agentic retrieval can return the JSON directly, so you don’t need a separate generation step. Validate the JSON in your code before you use it.

Give each audience its own persona and answerFormat, such as a customer answer and a ticket note, so the same knowledge bases can serve them all without mixing their formats.

Several retrievers can share one instruction version:.

Industry observers note that set identity, tone, and language once in persona, such as “Use a friendly, concise tone. Reply in the language of the question.”.

Put required lines in answerPolicy and citation forms in answerFormat, and give a realistic citation example, such as Source: central-returns-addendum.md, instead of a placeholder.

Use answerPolicy to name the fallback, such as “If the documents do not answer the question, say so and give the support contact.”.

According to recent reports, use retrievalGuidance for acronyms and preferred sources, such as “Treat model numbers as exact-match terms.” Check the Planning trace events to see how the agent searched. Use filters, not guidance, to limit what it retrieves.

Follow these practices when you write and roll out retrieval instructions:.

Sources indicate that to avoid ongoing charges, delete the retrieval instructions with the following commands. Then follow the cleanup steps in the repo README for the knowledge base, data source, S3 bucket, and roles.

It has been revealed that retrieval instructions give each tenant its own voice, answer format, date and money formats, and answer policy on shared managed knowledge bases. Pair them with metadata filters to keep tenant data apart and pinned versions to roll out changes one tenant at a time. The trace shows which version answered, and CloudTrail can record the AgenticRetrieveStream calls. Tag conditions add a check when tenants have their own credentials.

Industry observers note that to get started, see the AgenticRetrieveStream API reference and the GitHub repo. To learn more, read Agentic retrieval for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base.

  • These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-111357 Ivanti Connect Secure Missing Authentication for Critical Function Vulnerability CVE-2026-118527 Ivanti Connect Secure Generation of Predictable Numbers or Identifiers Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

CISA has added two upcoming vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities.
  • Recent findings suggest that our goal is to be exhaustive.
  • As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Recent findings suggest that our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:.

Sources indicate that every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Industry observers note that results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where latest models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:.

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:.

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:.

It has been revealed that -k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:.

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

#129. Breaking: Best practices for writing Denied Topics in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3105 w)

Breaking: Best practices for writing Denied Topics in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3105 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With Denied Topics in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, you block a content category by describing it in plain language, and the guardrail applies that description to every request by meaning rather than by keyword.
  • When Denied Topics blocks too much or too little, the cause is usually one of four authoring patterns:.
  • Recent findings suggest that the rest of this post is a practical guide to avoiding these patterns.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With Denied Topics in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, you block a content category by describing it in plain language, and the guardrail applies that description to every request by meaning rather than by keyword. That same mechanism can also match more than you intend. A topic named Finance, meant to keep an assistant out of investment advice, also blocks “When does my direct deposit clear?”. Inputs close in meaning to the topic can get caught, not only the requests you intended.

When Denied Topics blocks too much or too little, the cause is usually one of four authoring patterns:.

Recent findings suggest that the rest of this post is a practical guide to avoiding these patterns. It presents eight best practices for describing a topic precisely enough that the guardrail blocks what you mean and passes what you don’t.

To ground the following practices in something concrete, we use one running example throughout this post: a fictional bank we call AnyCompany Bank. AnyCompany Bank is two weeks from launching its first customer-facing AI assistant, and its first pass at the Denied Topics policy is blocking the wrong things.

According to recent reports, application: AnyCompany Bank’s chatbot is embedded in the AnyCompany Bank mobile and web app. It answers questions about accounts, statements, transfers, cards, and mortgages. It hands off to a human for account changes, dispute filings, and questions outside its scope.

Must-block list (from legal and compliance):.

Must-pass list (the things the assistant exists to do):.

Against that target, AnyCompany Bank’s team first drafted four topics, all of them right now blocking legitimate queries:.

Every one of these topics names a subject domain the assistant works in, rather than the intention the bank needs to refuse. Fixing this is what the rest of the post is about. The next eight sections work through the practices, most of them closing with a “Back at AnyCompany Bank” subsection that reveals the fix applied to this scenario. The post then closes with the one limitation to plan for regardless of how well you follow the practices: results are not fully deterministic.

According to recent reports, note: Denied Topic structure in Standard tier. A topic has three parts, a name, a definition, and up to five examples, and the guardrail evaluates all three together as a single unit, not the definition alone. The name can be up to 100 characters. The definition can be up to 1,000 characters, with 100–300 as the practical sweet spot. Each example can be up to 100 characters, and a guardrail can hold up to 30 topics.

It has been revealed that this practice sets the general frame. Best practices 2 through 4 apply it to each part of a topic in turn: the name, the definition, and the examples.

A frequent reason a topic blocks legitimate queries is that the topic describes a subject domain rather than what the user wants from the exchange. Two queries in the same domain can carry different intentions. “When does my direct deposit clear?” and “How much does an L5 engineer earn?” both concern pay, but only the second is a salary comparison. A domain-framed topic collapses those distinctions and can block queries semantically near the domain. A topic framed around the user’s intention matches only queries where that intention is present.

Intention is the framing lens. To make it operational, name the topic after the specific action or content type that expresses the intention on the surface, such as a request, a claim, or a piece of generated content. Intention tells you what to catch, and action gives you a concrete shape the guardrail can evaluate.

The guardrail evaluates both the topic name and its definition together. When either component names a domain, the topic matches too broadly. When both name an action that expresses a specific intention, the topic is precise.

Recent findings suggest that the next few best practices apply this idea to AnyCompany Bank’s own topics, with concrete examples. Best practice 2 renames them, and Best practice 3 tightens their definitions to match.

The topic name has a meaningful effect on what is matched, often greater than expected. A broad category name (Finance, Security, Legal) can lead the guardrail to associate the topic with vocabulary in that category, even when the definition attempts to narrow the scope. A specific action name (Investment Recommendations, Hacking Instructions, Suing for Damages) helps narrow the scope before the definition is read.

One of AnyCompany Bank’s first-draft topics was named Legal:.

In a recent development, this is why “Can you help me modify my mortgage?” got blocked. Mortgages are legal instruments, so queries about them live in the semantic neighborhood of legal. Renaming solves half the problem before we even touch the definition:.

The new name uses a verb-derived noun (litigation), names a second specific behavior (non-servicing legal advice), and makes clear by contrast that servicing questions, such as modifications, forbearance, and escrow, are outside the topic. The name itself now carries some of the work the definition would otherwise do alone.

AnyCompany Bank applied the same logic to the Fraud topic, renaming it to Fraud Investigation Requests. The assistant should still let customers report fraud, which gets routed to a human, but must not attempt to investigate fraud claims itself.

After these three renames, AnyCompany Bank’s topic list is:.

The definition should describe the user’s action on a specific object, rather than the general subject of that action.

We recommend the following structure:[Action or content-type opener] for [specific objects] by [qualifying constraint or purpose]. Includes [one or two sub-cases].

AnyCompany Bank’s first-draft topic was named Finance, with a definition to match:.

This is exactly why “Where can I find my payoff quote?” was blocked. Payoff is a financial term, quote concerns money, and the input is “related to” the finance domain, even though the customer’s intention, retrieving a servicing figure, has nothing to do with what AnyCompany Bank wanted to refuse.

Following Best practice 1, the team renamed the topic to Investment Recommendations and adjusted the definition’s vocabulary to match, without yet making it action-scoped:.

This was still domain-framed even though the name had improved. General education (“Explain what a mutual fund is”), historical financial news (“Why did rates rise last quarter?”), and portfolio review (“Show me my holdings”) all matched. The assistant should answer all of them.

The team applied the structural template, with an action opener, specific objects, a qualifying constraint, and one or two sub-cases:.

Every piece of the template serves a specific purpose. “Asking for a personalized recommendation to…” is the action opener. “Stocks, bonds, mutual funds, ETFs, or cryptocurrencies” are the specific objects. “For the user’s own investment returns” is the qualifying constraint that excludes educational and third-party discussion. The “Includes…” clause names two sub-cases: a specific-security question and an allocation-percentage question.

AnyCompany Bank applied the same template to the Litigation and Non-Servicing Legal Advice and Fraud Investigation Requests topics:.

The team now had three named topics with action-scoped definitions.

According to recent reports, examples teach the guardrail where the boundaries of your topic are. Not every example does this equally well. Five paraphrases of the same idea teach the guardrail nothing new, while five carefully chosen examples can draw the outline of the topic with much less definition text. The examples that carry the most weight are the ones sitting near the topic’s edge, close enough to a plausible non-match that they show the guardrail where to draw the line. We call these boundary examples. A good boundary example has three properties. First, it’s inside the topic’s scope. Second, it’s close to a plausible non-match, using vocabulary or structure that resembles inputs the topic should not match. Third, it differs from your other examples in sub-case, sentence shape, and vocabulary.

The team’s first pass at examples for Investment Recommendations looked like this:.

These are five ways of asking the same question. During testing, the assistant blocked “Should I buy stocks?” reliably. But it let through “Is it a good time to rotate my portfolio out of equities into bonds?”, which is exactly the kind of question the topic is supposed to catch. The paraphrases had crowded around one point in the topic, and other points were unguarded.

The rewrite spread the examples across sub-cases and sentence shapes:.

Recent findings suggest that these are five different sub-cases (specific stock, asset-class shift, allocation, sell timing, growth screen) and five different sentence shapes, all inside the topic. Adjacent non-matches like “Explain what an ETF is” (educational) and “Show me my portfolio report” (data retrieval) are sufficiently different from the examples that the guardrail should not match them.

Sources indicate that the team applied the same treatment to Litigation and Non-Servicing Legal Advice and Fraud Investigation Requests. The original Litigation examples were all variants of “Can I sue?” The rewritten set covered lawsuit filing, formal legal opinions, class-action inquiries, damages, and rights-interpretation. The original Fraud Investigation Requests examples were all variants of “Someone stole my money, what do I do?” The rewritten set covered unauthorized-charge investigation, card-fraud tracing, transaction reversal, identity-theft adjudication, and scammer tracing. Each rewritten set covers five different sub-cases inside one topic.

Recent findings suggest that at this point, AnyCompany Bank’s three topics pass every test written so far. One more problem only demonstrates up after the assistant runs against real traffic.

It has been revealed that some concepts are inherently ambiguous, because the same words describe both a matching and non-matching action, depending on context. In these cases, add an explicit anchor that fixes the context: an institutional setting, a stated purpose, or a dual condition of the form “only applies when both X and Y are present”.

According to recent reports, adding an insider-trading topic exposed the ambiguity issue. The compliance team wanted Insider Trading Advice as a distinct topic, narrower and more serious than the general Investment Recommendations catch. The first draft:.

This matched the expected case: a customer asking for a trade based on private information. It also matched something the team didn’t expect: educational queries about what insider trading is, phrased as questions. “How does the SEC define insider trading?” was getting blocked, because it “asks about insider trading”.

Both conditions should rule out educational queries: they fail condition 2, because they don’t describe non-public information the user personally holds. When the team tested “How does the SEC define insider trading?” against this definition, it still got blocked some of the time. The anchor was not the problem. The topic’s name was: it repeats the exact phrase the query uses. The guardrail weighs the name as a signal independent of the definition, the same effect Best practice 2 describes elsewhere. A dual-condition anchor can specify the right conditions and still lose to a name built from the term that it’s trying to disambiguate.

The team kept the anchor and renamed the topic instead:.

With the rename, the educational query passed reliably, and the real examples, the ones naming a specific security and a specific piece of non-public information, still blocked.

The definition is longer than the 100–300 character target from Best practice 3, and that is deliberate. The ambiguity here justifies the extra text. The topic itself is inherently subtle, so the definition has to carry more work.

A guardrail evaluates its topics together, not one at a time. When two topics have similar meanings, they interfere with each other. It becomes difficult to predict which topic the guardrail reports as the match, and the combined effect can block legitimate inputs that neither topic alone would block. Overlap between topics is often the reason a well-written topic produces incorrect results. The problem isn’t that topic, but a neighboring topic.

Sources indicate that suppose, late in the process, AnyCompany Bank’s compliance team proposed adding a broader Financial Advice topic alongside the already-defined Investment Recommendations. The intuition was that the broader topic would catch requests the specific one missed. Both topics were drafted with their own definitions:.

According to recent reports, the overlap became visible when the team tested “Should I put more into my 401(k)?”. Depending on how the caller ordered the topics in the API request, either Topic A, Topic B, or both would report the match, and on some orderings the guardrail blocked the input.

Industry observers note that anyCompany Bank consolidated. Financial Advice was removed, and Investment Recommendations was left to carry the specific action. After the consolidation, the ordering-dependent variance disappeared. The same input produced the same verdict regardless of where topics sat in the API call, which is the primary win from removing the overlap.

Sources indicate that the 401(k) query itself, however, was not fully resolved by consolidation alone. Because “Should I put more into my 401(k)?” shares its “Should I put more…” frame with a real trading recommendation, Investment Recommendations still matches it on the surface. This is a residual boundary case that consolidation can’t fix by itself. It’s exactly the kind of structurally-similar match that Best practice 8 warns a trailing exclusion can’t reliably override.

The team also reordered the remaining topics. The original order was:.

Sources indicate that topics 1 and 2 both discuss securities and cover related financial actions, so adjacent placement invited attribution ambiguity for borderline inputs. The team interleaved them:.

In a recent development, litigation and Non-Servicing Legal Advice now sits between the two securities-adjacent topics. Borderline questions like “Should I trade my Example Corp shares based on rumor?” now attribute more consistently to Trading on Non-Public Information rather than flipping between Trading on Non-Public Information and Investment Recommendations.

Denied Topics is the right tool when the rule you need to enforce is specific to your business and expressible as a short description of the content. Think of a regulatory line, a policy commitment, a legal risk, or a scope boundary, rather than a universal safety category or a fixed list of words. Guardrails offers several policies that share the same goal of blocking specific content, but each is designed for a different kind of signal. Using Denied Topics for a category that another policy handles natively tends to block too much or too little, complicates your configuration, and produces worse results. A carefully written topic for a category that Content Filter already covers is usually less effective than Content Filter for that category.

Recent findings suggest that note that enabling more than one policy in the same guardrail incurs additional cost, because each enabled policy is evaluated on every request. When you compose Denied Topics with Content Filter or Prompt Attack, plan for the combined cost.

Looking back at AnyCompany Bank’s must-block list (from the scenario at the start of the post), three of the six items are not really Denied Topics at all. They belong to policies that Guardrails already provides natively.

After this cleanup, AnyCompany Bank’s guardrail configuration composes multiple policies:.

Denied Topics carries only the four bank-specific rules that no other policy can express.

The following patterns cause topics to block the wrong inputs even when the rest of the definition is otherwise well written. Avoid them. Most are a specific case of guidance already given in earlier best practices, so each line that follows points back to where the full reasoning lives.

Recent findings suggest that A short trailing exclusion isn’t a general-purpose fix for every false refusal. It reliably rules out queries that are categorically different from the topic, such as a different intent, a different asker, or a different type of content. It’s less reliable when a benign query is worded almost exactly like the definition’s positive language, only about a different object. In that case, the exclusion competes against wording it closely resembles, and the match often wins.

For that structurally-similar case, prefer one of these three alternatives instead:.

A trailing exclusion remains the right first move for every other case. Reach for one of these three only when testing indicates the exclusion is losing to a near-identical match.

It has been revealed that even a guardrail that follows every practice in this post won’t produce fully deterministic results across every possible input. Denied Topics reads meaning with a language model, and language-model evaluations carry some inherent variance. There are two forms of this variance you should initiative for.

Industry observers note that variance when repeating the exact same request. Sending the identical input to the identical guardrail configuration two times in a row can, in rare cases, produce different results. The same characters go in, the same topic list applies, everything is the same, and yet one call blocks and the next passes. For most inputs, and for topics that follow the preceding guidance, this doesn’t happen, and the result is stable across repeated calls. The exceptions are borderline inputs, whose meaning sits close to the semantic edge of a topic. Those are the ones prone to flipping on repeat. The more precisely a topic is defined (action-scoped, specific objects, clear anchor, boundary examples), the fewer of your inputs fall in that borderline zone.

Sources indicate that variance when the topic list changes. The guardrail evaluates all topics together with the input on every request. Changes to the topic list, such as adding a topic, removing one, or reordering the same topics, can shift results for previously-tested inputs. An input that was blocked with one topic list might pass with a different one. This effect happens more when two topics share meaning or when a topic definition is broad. It happens less when every topic in the list has a specific, action-scoped definition and clear boundary examples. Applying the practices in this post meaningfully reduces both forms of variance.

Note: Every pass-or-fail claim in this post was tested end-to-end against Amazon Bedrock Guardrails (Standard tier), each query repeated multiple times to confirm the result was stable.

To recap, the practices in this post come down to eight points:.

Recent findings suggest that denied Topics is a powerful policy. With it, you can describe a bespoke content category in a short natural-language definition, without training a classifier or hand-crafting regular expressions. That power depends on describing the category the way the guardrail reads it: as the user’s intention, expressed as a specific action on a specific object, not as a subject domain. Get the framing right and the rest of the practices in this post, such as naming, definition, examples, anchors, overlap management, and policy selection, fall into place naturally.

To apply this in your own application:.

To get started, visit the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails console and the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails documentation for the full policy reference and API details, including CreateGuardrail and ApplyGuardrail.

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (445 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Cisa

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.
  • CISA has added one fresh vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.
  • This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-119977 WordPress Core Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition Vulnerability This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not right now listed in the KEV Catalog? #126. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1727 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1727 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one.
  • Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language.
  • Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It has been revealed that it lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

Industry observers note that it makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one claims, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:.

In a recent development, each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

According to recent reports, there's no public corpus of looks, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

It has been revealed that every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and indicates why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:.

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance.".

The coder reasons about geometry:.

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart.".

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

In a recent development, the hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Consumers often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:.

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

It has been revealed that the model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Sources indicate that even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

Recent findings suggest that first, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

In a recent development, figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

According to recent reports, to measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a blueprint, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Sources indicate that figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Recent findings suggest that palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

According to recent reports, presentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

Sources indicate that we also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:.

#120. Breaking: Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1294 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1294 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.
  • In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms.
  • It has been revealed that OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

It has been revealed that OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Sources indicate that run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

According to recent reports, A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that promptly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

Industry observers note that so we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:.

It has been revealed that the choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Sources indicate that either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:.

According to recent reports, all three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

According to recent reports, cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

According to recent reports, on a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

It has been revealed that A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

It has been revealed that this isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

According to recent reports, parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

  • CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-reference list to help organizations assess vendor readiness for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-reference list to help organizations assess vendor readiness for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). As quantum computing advances, widely used public-key cryptography will become vulnerable to compromise from cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs). To protect their systems and data, organizations must plan for and transition to PQC—which includes algorithms capable of withstanding both classical computing and quantum-enabled threats—before CRQCs become available. Many organizations rely on third-party vendors for managed services, cloud capabilities, and other cryptography-dependent products and services. Cryptography is also embedded in systems and devices that are difficult to patch, tied to long asset lifecycles, and require vendor support or replacement—such as industrial control systems and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. Reliance on vendors means that effective PQC transition depends on vendor readiness, and early, structured engagement with these vendors is critical to planning efforts. Organizations can use the vendor-neutral questions outlined in this guidance to determine whether a vendor understands quantum-related risks, maintains transparency over its cryptographic implementations, and supports a secure, cost-effective and timely transition to PQC. Visit CISA’s PQC Initiative page for additional resources.
