Latest Update: Decision Models in Hugging Face

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2165 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text.
  • Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:.
  • Recent findings suggest that "I was charged twice for my subscription.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:.

Recent findings suggest that "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today.".

The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?

This is the key idea behind decision models.

A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

Sources indicate that typeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

According to recent reports, the community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models).

For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:.

We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

However, there are a few problems with this approach.

Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:.

According to recent reports, A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.

Recent findings suggest that if we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.

In a recent development, zero-shot classification addresses an key part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

According to recent reports, unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

It has been revealed that decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.

Consider these three approaches:.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

A decision model request has the following two components:.

The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

Industry observers note that questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:.

Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.

Which department should handle this customer request?

The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.

The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z1,…,zKz_1,\ldots,z_Kz1​,…,zK​, (with KKK classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:.

pi=exp⁡(zi)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} pi​=∑j=1K​exp(zj​)exp(zi​)​.

Here, KKK is the number of choices.

Consider this illustrative distribution:.

According to recent reports, ∑i=1Kpi=1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i=1∑K​pi​=1.

The model chooses the option with the largest probability:.

y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y^​=argimax​pi​.

In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.

It has been revealed that choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?

How urgent is this customer request?

The model again produces a probability distribution:.

Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.

For a random variable XXX representing the level, the expectation is:.

E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E[X]=i=0∑K−1​ipi​.

E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7.

The reported score is therefore 1.7.

Recent findings suggest that this does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.

The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.

Is the customer requesting a refund?

Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).

Let YYY represent a binary outcome:.

Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y∼Bernoulli(p).

Industry observers note that P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p. P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.

it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No.

The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.

So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score.

The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that.

For a Choice with KKK options, the confidence is:.

pmax⁡−1K1−1K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1−K1​pmax​−K1​​.

where pmax⁡p_{\max}pmax​ is the largest predicted probability.

In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.998:.

C=3(0.998)−12=0.997 C=\frac{3(0.998)-1}{2}=0.997 C=23(0.998)−1​=0.997.

According to recent reports, notice that the winning probability is 0.998, but the reported confidence is 0.997. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.

It has been revealed that decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:.

The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.

Recent findings suggest that transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline, AutoModelForDecision, and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models.

One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:.

Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint.

We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:.

Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:.

The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.

An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a latest model.

llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API.

For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:.

The default server runs on port 9931.

In a recent development, we can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request.

The useful property is interface compatibility.

Hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.

For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.

It has been revealed that once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API.

Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it reveals the parts that matter:.

Sources indicate that first-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.

If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is upcoming, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.

Industry observers note that great write-up. The step the post leaves to the application, turning noul: 0.83 into an action, is where things get hard in production. It's usually a threshold (if p > 0.9), and it quietly goes stale: raw probabilities are rarely calibrated, the right cut-off depends on what a mistake costs, and the outcome that claims whether the decision was right (a chargeback, a reassigned ticket) arrives days or months later.

I'm building an open-source, self-hosted tool for that loop: trimset. It sits in front of any /v1/systemone server (so transformers serve or llama.cpp) with a one-line URL change. It logs every decision and joins the real outcome when it arrives. It calibrates per question and model, then compiles thresholds and an escalation band with a stated guarantee ("false passes ≤ 2% with 95% confidence"), which your app applies locally. It's pre-alpha; drift and silent-upgrade alerts come next.

Live demo on recorded data, threshold simulator included: https://demo.trimset.dev/#/questions/refund_fraud/simulator.

For anyone running decision models in production: how do you pick your cut-offs today?

"Not because x, but because y" is very AI-sloppy language.

In a recent development, the advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface.

Recent findings suggest that nobody thinks that, literally. What I mean by that is, nothing capable of thinking would have written this sentence down because no thinking entity would suspect that decision models originated probabilistic classification. Only a non-thinking source of language, such as an LLM, might generate this sentence.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Again, nobody thinks that, meaning only an LLM might generate this sentence.

Sources indicate that the state + questions interface carries over to hosted decision models too. meraGPT Decider 1.1 takes the same shape through an API (model decider-1.1) rather than as open weights: up to 255 options per choice question, images in the state, and if you offer an "I don't know" option it takes it when the state doesn't support an answer. Tech Report: How MoEngage built agentic customer engagement on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1866 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This post was co-written with Ashwin Srinivasan, Nishan Das and Karthik Baile from MoEngage.
  • It has been revealed that A marketing or product team member planning a weekend flash sale often opens three tools before writing a single line of copy.
  • The MoEngage Model Context Protocol (MCP) Connector gives an MCP-compatible assistant, such as Claude or ChatGPT, secure, tenant-scoped access to a brand’s segments, campaign history, and content library.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This post was co-written with Ashwin Srinivasan, Nishan Das and Karthik Baile from MoEngage.

It has been revealed that A marketing or product team member planning a weekend flash sale often opens three tools before writing a single line of copy. First they open the analytics dashboard to see what worked last time, then the content library to find the right tone, and then the campaign builder to build the campaign itself. Repeat that across email, push, SMS, and WhatsApp, and much of a marketing team’s week goes to navigating tools instead of making decisions.

The MoEngage Model Context Protocol (MCP) Connector gives an MCP-compatible assistant, such as Claude or ChatGPT, secure, tenant-scoped access to a brand’s segments, campaign history, and content library.

This capability points to a broader shift in software platforms. Beyond a user interface for business owners and an API for engineering teams, a third layer is emerging, where a user describes an outcome in plain language and an agent carries out the steps across the platform. For a customer engagement platform, that means a capability already exposed as an API can become a tool an agent calls, and a campaign that once moved across several tools can move through one conversation instead.

In a recent development, moEngage, the agentic customer engagement platform that more than 1,350 consumer brands use across channels including push, email, in-app, SMS, WhatsApp, and Rich Communication Services (RCS), set out to build this layer. MoEngage built Merlin AI, a set of artificial intelligence (AI) agents that work with live platform data. Marketing and product teams can now draft, analyze, and adjust campaigns from a single conversation, while agents decide what to send each customer. One customer, Glance, saw a 38% uplift in push notification click-through rates as a result.

It has been revealed that moEngage treated this as an architecture problem. The question was how to give agents secure, tenant-scoped access to live data without rebuilding hundreds of existing APIs. In this post, we walk through how MoEngage solved it with Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize AI agents at scale with any framework or model. The post covers the four agent modes in Merlin AI, how MoEngage exposed its existing APIs as MCP tools, and how the architecture keeps each tenant’s data isolated. It closes with the results MoEngage customers have seen and the pattern other software providers can reuse.

It has been revealed that merlin AI runs four kinds of agents. All four share the same foundation: foundation models in Amazon Bedrock for reasoning and generation, AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, for hosting, and MCP for standardized access to data. Across all four modes, Merlin AI uses Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock for reasoning, tool-call planning, and content generation. For the full list of models, see Supported foundation models in Amazon Bedrock.

Merlin AI Studio places purpose-built agents at the exact point in the workflow where marketing and product teams do that piece of work:.

According to recent reports, conversational agents work across campaigns, analytics, segments, and flows. A user can ask a question in plain language and the agent calls the right tools to answer it or act on it. The Campaign Insights Agent, embedded on the analytics page, delegates to specialized sub-agents. One sub-agent runs analysis across several metrics at once. A second diagnoses why a metric is underperforming, and a third compares performance across time periods or segments. A final step formats the findings into a clear answer.

Custom agents let lifecycle and customer relationship management (CRM) teams design agents that run continuously on MoEngage data and tools, inside rules the product and marketing team defines. Every agent reveals its work through an activity log of the data it pulled, the decisions it made, the channels it touched, and the content it sent. Teams can run an agent with full autonomy or require human review before anything executes.

It has been revealed that decisioning agents act for each individual customer. Each agent decides what to say, when, how often, and on which channel, and it learns from every outcome. Product and marketing teams set the content, goals, and guardrails, and the agents handle the rest, with visibility into every decision. Offer Decisioning selects the best offer on web and app surfaces. Campaign Decisioning delivers 1:1 decisions across email, push, SMS, and WhatsApp. Together with workflow agents, this puts both halves of agentic marketing in one system.

The architecture has four layers. Each layer has a single responsibility and can change without affecting the others.

In a recent development, in a typical request, a user signs in to MoEngage and asks a question. The client sends the request with the user’s existing JSON Web Token (JWT). AgentCore runtime validates the token and starts an isolated session for that user. The agent asks a model in Amazon Bedrock which tools to call. The MCP server calls the MoEngage APIs with the user’s tenant context and returns the results. The agent then composes the answer.

The following diagram shows how these components connect.

Figure 1: MoEngage Merlin AI architecture on Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore runtime.

MoEngage opens its platform to agents through an MCP server and agent-callable APIs. Its platform APIs for campaigns, analytics, segments, content, and flows were already OpenAPI 3.0-compatible, so MoEngage used the FastMCP framework to generate MCP tools from those specifications. Each operation becomes a tool with a structured schema, a description, and parameter validation.

The following simplified example shows the pattern:.

The tools fall into five groups:.

The tools come from the specifications, so they stay in sync with the APIs. When a team updates a specification, the tool definitions patch with it.

Recent findings suggest that A multi-tenant system cannot let a model decide whose data it is reading. MoEngage made three design choices to help prevent that. First, the MCP server reuses the existing authentication model, accepting the same JWT-based authentication that MoEngage APIs already use, and AgentCore runtime validates each token before a request reaches the server. Second, workspace and user context travel in request headers that AgentCore runtime forwards to the server rather than as tool arguments, so the model does not see these values and cannot change them. Third, AgentCore runtime runs each user session in its own isolated environment, so one user’s conversation cannot read another’s session state.

On top of this, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails apply content safety and personally identifiable information (PII) filters to agent responses. A backend-for-frontend layer then validates the structure of generated content before the MoEngage interface renders it.

Sources indicate that give users control over agents. Users set guardrails on what each agent can do, review every action in its activity log, and choose between autonomous and human-reviewed execution.

AgentCore runtime provides the production capabilities that a multi-tenant MCP server needs, and each one addresses a specific requirement of MoEngage’s workload. AgentCore runtime scales sessions as demand changes, so MoEngage does not proposal capacity for traffic bursts across its customer workspaces. Each session runs in its own isolated environment by default, which keeps one brand’s conversation and data separate from another’s. The built-in JWT authorizer validates tokens against MoEngage’s existing identity provider, so the MCP server uses the same authentication model as the APIs.

Hosting on AgentCore runtime is also framework-agnostic. MoEngage can change models or agent frameworks without touching the MCP server, which matters as the agent layer evolves. Built-in metrics, logs, and traces through Amazon CloudWatch give MoEngage engineers visibility into every session. Together, these capabilities let the team focus on agent logic and marketing intelligence rather than hosting infrastructure.

In a recent development, inference through Amazon Bedrock gave MoEngage two more benefits. Merlin AI agents run on Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock, and MoEngage moves between these versions through the same Amazon Bedrock API. MoEngage also pays per token instead of operating GPU infrastructure. Amazon Bedrock does not use customer prompts or responses to train foundation models, which matters for a system that processes customer engagement data at scale.

The following example shows how a user builds a campaign without leaving the conversation.

Draft a weekend flash sale push for our high-value segment, using the same tone as our best-performing December campaign.

It has been revealed that the agent calls the analytics tools to find the top December campaign, the segmentation tools to confirm the high-value segment, and the content tools to pull the brand voice. It returns a draft with several copy variants.

Which push notifications last month had below 2% click-through rate (CTR), and what do they have in common?

The Campaign Insights Agent compares those campaigns and reports the shared pattern, such as send time or audience overlap.

Show me the drop-off at step 3 of our onboarding flow, and pause the SMS branch if it’s below 5% conversion.

According to recent reports, the agent reads the flow state through the flow tools and pauses the branch after the user confirms. This is the human-review mode in practice.

Each step uses the same tools that power the MoEngage interface. The user does not open a separate dashboard.

Merlin AI agents on this architecture have been in production for more than 6 months. One customer, Glance, reached campaign go-live 50% faster and saw a 38% uplift in push notification click-through rates. With Merlin AI Copywriter, Glance teams also produce about three times more content variants per campaign.

Across the platform, MoEngage reports a 60–70% reduction in manual effort by marketing and product teams for channel, timing, and frequency decisions, and a 20–30% improvement in conversion rates from goal-based decisioning. Managed, pay-per-token inference in Amazon Bedrock reduced AI infrastructure costs by more than 50% compared with self-hosted models.

Sources indicate that agentCore feature availability varies by AWS Region. For supported Regions, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation.

MoEngage made its platform agent-ready without rebuilding it. Existing OpenAPI specifications became MCP tools. AgentCore runtime provided hosting, authentication, and session isolation. Foundation models in Amazon Bedrock provided reasoning and generation. The result is a platform where marketing and product teams move from question to action in one conversation, where MoEngage engineers spend their time on marketing intelligence rather than infrastructure, and where agents handle workflows for the team and decisions for every customer while users stay in control.

The same pattern applies to other software providers with a mature API surface. Start from your existing specifications, keep identity outside the model, and let a managed runtime handle the production concerns.

Sources indicate that to build your own MCP server on the same foundation, start with the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation and follow the AgentCore runtime guide to host it. To choose a foundation model for your agents and review the security and data-handling controls, see the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. To generate MCP tools from your existing OpenAPI specifications, review the FastMCP documentation. To see Merlin AI in action, visit MoEngage Merlin AI. To strategy a similar architecture, contact your AWS account team or Solutions Architect.

View CSAF Summary Palo Alto Networks has published information on vulnerabilities in PAN-OS related to PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. This advisory lists the related Siemens Industrial products affected by these vulnerabilities. Customers are advised to consult and implement the workarounds provided in Palo Alto Networks' upstream security notifications. The following versions of Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 are affected: RUGGEDCOM APE1808 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 9.8 Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 1 Vulnerability Use After Free Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-109618 PHP uses longjmp() for out-of-memory (OOM) errors to exit the current context and abort handling of the request. Some contexts may not properly account for this scenario and leave request memory in an uninitialized state before performing an allocation. The subsequent request cleanup procedure may read or branch on this memory. Multiple OOM strategies can consistently trigger this condition and lead to remote code execution (RCE). Read More 1 Affected Product RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS (10.2 All, 11.1 All, 11.2 All, 12.1 All, 12.2 All) Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fixUpgrade to corresponding available PAN-OS version. Contact customer support to receive additional patch and patch information. Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-416 Use After Free CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 9.8 CRITICAL CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H View CVE Details CVE-2026-109619 PHP has various global state that temporarily points into request memory. In some scenarios, global state may not be correctly reset, or may be repopulated after being reset. The global state may then refer to request memory even after it has been freed. Subsequent requests may read or branch on this stale state before it is fully initialized. Multiple strategies can trigger this condition and produce remote code execution (RCE). General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. Recommended Practices CISA recommends people take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. Industry observers note that you can now link your Hugging Face organization to your Google Cloud account, so that your Hugging Face usage reveals up on your Google Cloud bill instead of being charged to a credit card. Get started on the Google Cloud Marketplace.

Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with Jobs, deploying models with Inference Endpoints, calling thousands of models through Inference Providers, or hosting demos on GPU Spaces.

If your manufacturer already runs on Google Cloud, adding a latest vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace:.

If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step.

It has been revealed that you are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm.

In a recent development, you are then redirected to the billing settings of your organization. The payment method section now indicates the linked Google Cloud account, with a pending status.

Every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any.

Once your subscription is approved, you will receive an email confirming that your Google Cloud account and Hugging Face organization are linked. Organizations that already have a credit card on file switch to cloud marketplace billing at the start of their next billing period. Organizations on the free tier with no credit card on file usually switch immediately, so their paid usage is billed through the cloud marketplace right away.

To confirm it, open the billing settings of your organization: the Google Cloud account is now shown as the organization's active payment method.

Industry observers note that your organization is now billed through your Google Cloud account. All members of your organization can use Hugging Face compute services, and the usage will show up on your Google Cloud bill.

Recent findings suggest that thanks for reading! You can find more details in the billing documentation. If you have any questions, please contact us at billing@huggingface.co.

Industry observers note that view CSAF Summary On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write that could allow a remote attacker to cause memory corruption and potentially execute arbitrary code. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens software products. Siemens has released latest versions for the affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. The following versions of Siemens Desigo, Gridscale are affected: Desigo CC family V8 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497) Desigo CC family V9 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497) Gridscale X DSA vers:intdot/>=5.3|<5.4 (CVE-2026-111497) Gridscale X PSS®E vers:intdot/<36.8.0 (CVE-2026-111497)   CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 9.8 Siemens Desigo CC family V8 1 Vulnerability Out-of-bounds Write Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Information Technology Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-111497 A buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c) in Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream. Users need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries between 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 to the latest available version: 1.0.10 or 1.1.1 or 1.2.1. General Recommendations Operators of critical power systems (e.g. TSOs or DSOs) worldwide are usually required by regulations to build resilience into the power grids by applying multi-level redundant secondary protection schemes. It is therefore recommended that the operators check whether appropriate resilient protection measures are in place. The risk of cyber incidents impacting the grid's reliability can thus be minimized by virtue of the grid design. Siemens strongly recommends applying the provided security updates using the corresponding tooling and documented procedures made available with the product. If supported by the product, an automated means to apply the security updates across multiple product instances may be used. Siemens strongly recommends prior validation of any security update before being applied, and supervision by trained staff of the update process in the target environment. As a general security measure Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access with appropriate mechanisms (e.g. firewalls, segmentation, VPN). It is advised to configure the environment according to our operational guidelines in order to run the devices in a protected IT environment. Recommended security guidelines can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/gridsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CVE-2026-114713 UnrealIRCd Improper Neutralization of Delimiters Vulnerability CVE-2026-123039 Check Point Multiple Products Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not presently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

#57. Taxonomy of multi-agent design patterns, anti-patterns, and lessons from manufacturing

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2478 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Taxonomy of multi-agent design patterns, anti-patterns, and lessons from manufacturing

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2478 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Enterprise teams are building multi-agent systems, and when early implementations fall short, the cause is rarely the model.
  • The numbers are consistent across sources: ~88% of AI pilots never reach production.
  • Recent findings suggest that in this post, you learn how to decide whether a use case needs multiple agents, choose a coordination pattern, and spot costly anti-patterns early.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Enterprise teams are building multi-agent systems, and when early implementations fall short, the cause is rarely the model. Multi-agent coordination is a distributed systems problem, and many teams taking it on haven’t yet built distributed systems instincts.

The numbers are consistent across sources: ~88% of AI pilots never reach production. Stanford HAI demonstrated that two models can perform worse collaborating than either alone when coordination overhead exceeds the benefit. The pattern is clear: teams are adding complexity faster than they build understanding. Ten steps that are each 95 percent reliable deliver only 59.9 percent end-to-end reliability, and 20 steps deliver 35.8 percent. This illustrative model assumes a strictly sequential chain with no retries, but the direction holds: each dependent handoff multiplies risk.

Recent findings suggest that in this post, you learn how to decide whether a use case needs multiple agents, choose a coordination pattern, and spot costly anti-patterns early. You also see how takt time, safety boundaries, edge data, and shift cycles shape the architecture.

Coordination patterns fall into two tiers, based on who controls the flow. In Tier 1, you define the path.

In Tier 2, the model chooses the path at runtime. That flexibility handles work whose steps you can’t define in advance, at a higher cost in tokens, latency, and debugging. The practical default is to start with Tier 1 and move a task to Tier 2 only when its subtasks emerge during the work.

1.1 Sequential Pipeline: Orchestration patterns that implement linear execution where each node’s output feeds into the next node (A -> B -> C) supporting ordered processing with predictable execution timing.

In the following diagram, input flows to agent A (extract), then agent B (transform), then agent C (validate), and then output. The user defines that order at build time, and nothing is decided at runtime. As a result, the pipeline is straightforward to debug and test, and its cost is predictable. Typical fits include document processing, extract, transform, and load (ETL) chains, and warranty-claim triage.

Figure 1: Sequential pipeline where each agent’s output feeds the next, from extract to transform to validate.

1.2 Conditional Workflow: Logic-based edges select the next node by condition, so the workflow can branch and send each case down a different path.

Recent findings suggest that in the following diagram, a user request goes to agent A (write code) and then to agent B (test code). A pass/fail check sends passing work to agent D (deploy). Failing work loops back to agent A for a retry, up to a maximum of N times, and then escalates to a human. The orchestration layer enforces that cap, for example through an AWS Step Functions iteration limit, which keeps the loop from becoming the unbounded iteration anti-pattern described later in this post.

Figure 2: Conditional workflow that retries failures up to N times before escalating to a human.

In a recent development, A classification step examines the input and directs it to the appropriate processing path. Only one path is executed per request. Best for intent-driven dispatch, quality-gate decisions, customer inquiry routing, and anomaly triage.

According to recent reports, the following diagram shows a plant supervisor’s request being read by a classifier and sent to exactly one specialist. Questions about whether parts meet spec go to the Quality Agent, overdue equipment services go to the Maintenance Agent, and shift changes go to the Scheduling Agent. This decision is made at the entry point.

Figure 3: Conditional router that runs one path per request, with bounded retries before human escalation.

It has been revealed that 1.4 Parallel Workflow: A task splits into independent subtasks that run simultaneously across handlers, each on its own data. A fan-in step combines the results when all handlers complete, and a failure in one path retries only that path. Best for multi-source analysis, batch processing, and work that decomposes into independent pieces.

Industry observers note that in the following diagram, a research orchestrator decomposes the task and dispatches it to three specialist agents that run concurrently: a financial data agent, a geopolitical agent, and a logistics agent, each analyzing its own source. A combined step waits for all three, then synthesizes the results, resolves conflicts, and ranks the findings. Latency equals the slowest single agent rather than the sum of all three.

Figure 4: Parallel fan-out to specialist agents followed by a fan-in step that synthesizes and ranks the results.

Industry observers note that in autonomous patterns, control flow is determined at runtime by the AI model itself, not predefined by developers. Agents read task state, reason about what’s needed and coordinate through shared context rather than fixed paths spanning a spectrum from structured orchestration to fully emergent behavior.

It has been revealed that in strategy-based orchestration, a single orchestrator agent acts as a project manager. The orchestrator maintains an explicit task plan with assignments and dependencies, sees all context while each worker receives only its slice, distributes work dynamically against the current plan, and monitors progress centrally. Key design choice is that the workers are stateless and independent. If one fails, it doesn’t contaminate others. The orchestrator retries only the failed worker, not the entire workflow.

The following diagram reveals how a planner agent decomposes a task into an explicit initiative and dispatches each step to a worker’s agent. Each step goes to a dedicated worker (a research agent, an analysis agent, and a report agent) that sees only its assigned slice.

Figure 5: Initiative-based orchestration with a planner agent assigning each step to a stateless worker agent.

Agents operate with limited, local knowledge and coordinate through peer-to-peer delegation. Each makes local decisions about when and to whom to transfer control, based on the task and the agents it knows. Control passes with state: each transfer carries validated task state, the evidence behind it, and any unresolved questions, so the receiving agent continues rather than reinterpreting a summary. A handoff that moves only through the conversation is not a handoff.

Industry observers note that in the following diagram, a customer service agent transfers control, together with its context, to either a technical support agent or a billing agent, and technical support can hand off further to a senior engineer. Each agent knows only the small set of peers it can transfer to.

Figure 6: Handoff pattern passing validated state between peer agents through local delegation.

In conversation-driven patterns (also known as group chat patterns), all agents participate in a shared conversation where orchestration emerges through turn-taking rather than explicit looks or structured handoffs. This mirrors human team collaboration where everyone can see the discussion and contribute when appropriate.

In the following diagram, an agent-selection mechanism decides whose turn it is, and agents A, B, and C each add to one shared conversation, where every turn is a message plus a tool call. The selection mechanism sets the turn-taking, and state lives implicitly in the conversation history.

Figure 7: Conversation-driven pattern where turn-taking selects the next agent and state lives in the conversation.

Multiple agents independently evaluate the same input, and their conclusions are reconciled by majority, by a judge agent, or by escalation when they disagree. Unlike a conversation-driven pattern, the agents do not see each other’s reasoning before committing to a position, which is what makes disagreement informative rather than socially convergent.

It has been revealed that use it sparingly. Debate is the most expensive pattern here, and on perceptual tasks it buys latency rather than accuracy (see the quality-inspection case in anti-pattern 3 that follows). Reserve it for high-stakes, low-volume decisions where being wrong costs more than deliberating.

In practice, most production systems combine several patterns based on task decomposition:.

The governing principle: pattern-to-task alignment. Match the orchestration approach to each task’s inherent characteristics and your system’s reliability requirements rather than forcing everything through a single pattern.

Each of the following five anti-patterns looks reasonable at design time, and each surfaces later as an inflated token cost, a missed takt-time window, or a decision that has quietly drifted out of sync with the plant floor.

According to recent reports, one agent owns overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) analysis, programmable logic controller (PLC) diagnostics, and maintenance behind a single prompt with 15 or more tools. Tool selection degrades as tools grow, and failures become hard to attribute.

The fix: Bounded agents of five tools or fewer, such as an OEE analyst, a fault diagnostician, and a maintenance drafter.

Industry observers note that the agent loops on “try again” with no hard stop. A four-agent system can burn a significantly higher number of tokens before a single retry, and no one call trips an alarm. Retries multiply coordination failures rather than fixing them.

It has been revealed that the fix: Hard iteration ceiling in code, per-agent token ceiling, budget alarm wired to an automatic stop. Infrastructure enforces limits. The model will not stop itself.

It has been revealed that agents hand each other free-text prose with no schema. Interpretation hardens at every hop: “could indicate wear” becomes “confirmed wear” becomes a maintenance order. The drift happens between agents, where tracing is thinnest.

Sources indicate that multi-agent where one agent with tool groups would do. Each agent adds a coordination tax that is not linear, and the gains flatten around four. Most “specialists” are one model in different costumes.

Industry observers note that the fix: Needs at least two different models, different tool access, concurrent execution, and real interdependency. Fewer than two, and one agent with action groups does it.

Recent findings suggest that the test: can one agent handle the phases by switching tools? Then it is not a multi-agent problem.

The agent triggers real-world actions (email, service visits, machine parameters) with no approval step. Hallucinations cross into the physical world, irreversible actions compound, and liability escalates from a refund to product liability.

The fix: Defense in depth: recommendation → Amazon Bedrock Guardrails → schema validation → business rules → human approval → execution.

Every point where agent output reaches a customer, or a safety system is a trust boundary.

With the patterns and anti-patterns in view, the architecture choice comes down to a short sequence of questions.

The following decision tree turns these four questions into a path you can follow from top to bottom.

Figure 8: Decision tree for choosing the simplest architecture, from a single model call to a Tier 2 multi-agent pattern.

The tree starts by asking whether the task requires actions beyond text generation. If it doesn’t, a simple model call is enough. If it does, the tree asks whether the solution is well known and can be expressed as a workflow. On the known solution side, work that benefits from specialized expertise or domain separation go to a Tier 1 multi-agent workflow (a pipeline, fan-out, or router). Everything else goes to a single agent with tools and action groups. On the unknown-solution side, only tasks that involve exploration or significant side effects go to Tier 2 for autonomous multi-agent patterns. The rest stays with a single agent. The guiding principle is to choose the simplest architecture that meets your requirements.

According to recent reports, the following chart compares the patterns on four things: when to reach for each one, how control flows between agents, how deterministic the result is, and what it costs to build and operate. Build cost is a relative scale, not an estimate.

Figure 9: Comparison of the patterns by use case, control flow, determinism, and relative build cost.

Sources indicate that tier 1 patterns score high on determinism at low to moderate build cost. Tier 2 patterns give more of the path to the model, and proposal-based orchestration costs the most to build. If you can draw the control flow on a whiteboard before runtime, start with Tier 1.

Manufacturing is not a generic enterprise IT environment, and four constraints make that arithmetic unforgiving.

Automotive body shops, where robots weld the vehicle body together, typically run at 60 jobs per hour. Each of their over 40 stations has a 60-second takt time before the line advances. Inference latency that sits on a station’s cycle path eats into those 60 seconds, and a delay at the bottleneck station slows the whole line. Even a 2 percent throughput reduction can translate to significant annual revenue impact.

Architecture implication: budget latency at p99, not average. The tail is what stops the line. Give every agent a sub-second deterministic fallback, and match it to the risk:.

A hallucinated chatbot causes embarrassment. A hallucinated welding parameter causes structural defects that surface in crash testing or field failure and can lead to a safety recall. Two failure modes recur:.

The boundary: keep the deterministic core unchanged, including PLCs, supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems, and the MES, and wrap an advisory layer around it.

Validation and approval: A recommendation passes schema validation and physics simulation, checked against the OT source of truth immediately before actuation, never against OT state cached beyond one cycle. It’s then approved at a level matched to its scope:.

Sources indicate that only then does a validated command interface pass permitted commands to deterministic control. The large language model (LLM) proposes. The physics engine and the human operator dispose.

In a recent development, A single stamping press generates 50+ GB/day of sensor data whose value decays in milliseconds. Shipping it to the cloud costs more in bandwidth than compute, and by the time the cloud answers, the press has moved on.

Architecture implication: hybrid edge-cloud is the practical default, and the Constraint 2 boundary holds at the edge too.

Sources indicate that unbounded context makes an agent drift as stale observations crowd out current reality. A full reset loses continuity between shifts. Manufacturing already solves this for humans with structured shift handoffs, and agents need the same discipline.

Architecture implication: Bound agent memory to the shift cycle.

The following managed services map to the concerns raised earlier in this post. Each row names the mechanism, not just the service.

Multi-agent systems change how automotive manufacturers orchestrate intelligence at scale, but only when built on the right foundations.

According to recent reports, the patterns and anti-patterns here come from real deployments where poor architecture indicates up as runaway token costs, takt-time violations, and, at worst, physical safety risks. The economics at plant scale are unforgiving, because token volume grows with every agent, robot, and shift. Tiered model selection, context compression, and edge-cloud distribution are the main levers for delivering the same value at a fraction of that cost.

The recommendation here is to start with Tier 1 patterns, prove value, and then expand. Most manufacturing use cases, such as shift handoff summarization, quality-gate decisions, and predictive maintenance, are well served by deterministic workflows. Reserve autonomous orchestration for genuinely open-ended problems where dynamic subtask discovery justifies the added cost, latency, and debugging complexity.

#54. Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1971 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1971 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document.
  • Industry observers note that token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors.
  • Sources indicate that in this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up promptly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors!

Industry observers note that token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget.

Sources indicate that in this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4, my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how.

This post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study, which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example.

Recent findings suggest that pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below.

Recent findings suggest that A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document.

For example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together:.

MaxSim⁡(Q,D)=∑q∈Qmax⁡d∈Dq⊤d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim(Q,D)=q∈Q∑​d∈Dmax​q⊤d.

Even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID, storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision.

The useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together.

HierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering. Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors.

These merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring.

You can make compression proportional to document length:.

It has been revealed that with pool_factor=4, documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged.

HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls:.

According to recent reports, this distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4, a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold, the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved.

Sources indicate that adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective.

Industry observers note that rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents:.

Calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus.

Recent findings suggest that pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that.

It has been revealed that if you've used Matryoshka embeddings, the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors.

For my example, each training batch contributes two losses:.

L=12Lunpooled+12Lpooled \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unpooled}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pooled}} L=21​Lunpooled​+21​Lpooled​.

Industry observers note that the first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives update the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression.

According to recent reports, ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together. During training, HierarchicalTokenPooling uses a straight-through estimator to pass gradients from pooled vectors back to their member tokens, without differentiating the cluster assignments. The encoder can then learn from retrieval errors made with its pooled representations.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss wraps an existing multi-vector retrieval loss and applies it using your chosen poolers:.

In a recent development, cachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss supplies the retrieval objective. It teaches each query to score its relevant document above the negative documents in the batch. By default, it uses model.similarity, using the model's similarity setting (MaxSim in this example) and kernel settings. A model configured with similarity_fn_name="meanmaxsim" would also use MeanMaxSim during training.

Gradient caching allows the encoder to process small mini-batches while retaining a larger set of in-batch negatives. My training script uses mini-batches of 64 with a training batch size of 256.

Recent findings suggest that multiVectorTokenPoolingLoss adds the compression objective. Here, None means that one variant uses the original embeddings, while pooling supplies the factor-4 variant. The two weights average their losses. Pooling variants reuse the computed token embeddings, so each additional pooler adds clustering and scoring work without requiring a separate encoder pass for that variant.

Recent findings suggest that the poolers can also be custom BaseTokenPooling implementations that preserve gradients through their input embeddings. You can adapt the training objective to the representation you want to deploy.

Replace the factor-4 pooler with your chosen deployment configuration, or include several poolers and choose weights for their losses.

According to recent reports, the complete training script includes the dataset, trainer, validation loss, and small retrieval evaluations during training. From a checkout of the repository, run both variants locally with uv:.

The script declares its training and kernel dependencies, so uv installs them for you. Compatible kernels are enabled automatically.

This runs the pooling-aware variant on an A10G GPU with a four-hour time limit. Passing HF_TOKEN as a secret lets the script upload the trained model to your Hub account when training finishes. To run the ordinary-loss baseline as well, repeat the command with --baseline after the script URL.

In a recent development, you can accelerate MaxSim scoring, Ward clustering, and supported backbone operations with kernels. Install the training and kernel dependencies:.

In the training example above, replace the model and pooler initialization before constructing the loss:.

Hierarchical poolers inherit the model's kernel settings by default, so you only need to enable kernels on the model.

According to recent reports, sentence Transformers selects compatible kernels for your setup and uses the existing implementation wherever a replacement isn't available. For example, the default MaxSim kernel scores queries against documents without building the full token similarity matrix in memory, but it does require CUDA and Triton.

In a recent development, the default Ward clustering kernel considerably speeds up hierarchical clustering by running on CUDA instead of the CPU. We're talking about 30-150x faster than SciPy depending on the setting.

Let's load the pooling-aware model and retrieve with compressed document embeddings. Kernel settings aren't saved with the model, so add use_kernels=True when loading if you'd like to use them for inference too:.

The pooler compresses the document embeddings after the encoder's forward pipeline, reducing the total from 58 vectors to 16 while leaving query embeddings unchanged. Mars still receives the highest similarity score, followed by Jupiter and Venus, so the ranking is preserved despite storing far fewer document vectors.

You can change pool_factor at inference to explore a different storage budget with the same trained model. For repeated use, you can also pass token_pooling=pooling when initializing MultiVectorEncoder to make it the runtime default. The pooler's tasks still control which inputs are compressed (e.g. only documents).

To investigate, I trained two models from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, each with a fresh 128-dimensional token projection:.

Both runs use one epoch over the same 120,000 MS MARCO triplets, seed 42, and matching initialization and optimization settings. The training token cap is 300, and short queries are expanded to at least 32 token positions to provide additional contextual query vectors. Only the loss differs between the two experiments, and I didn't run a hyperparameter search.

I evaluated both models on NanoBEIR@13, reporting mean nDCG@10 (%). The figure compares ordinary and pooling-aware training with pool factors of 2, 3, 4, and 6, alongside unpooled retrieval. The table also includes fixed caps and adaptive thresholds, showing how the training benefits transfer to other pooling settings.

According to recent reports, for adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps.

In a recent development, at the trained pool_factor=4, nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39.

The gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget.

If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order:.

If the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus.

According to recent reports, multiVectorMatryoshkaLoss trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings.

Sources indicate that try the complete training example, choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model.

With a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical!
