#20. Build memory-aware AI agents with Agentic Retrieve on Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3418 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Build memory-aware AI agents with Agentic Retrieve on Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3418 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, customers of a knowledge-grounded application expect it to remember them, not only to search well.
  • Meeting that expectation is hard, because the context that would sharpen a search lives outside the knowledge base.
  • Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, now take over these steps: storing each conversation, extracting facts from it, and bringing the relevant facts into the search.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, customers of a knowledge-grounded application expect it to remember them, not only to search well. They ask follow-up questions that make sense only in the context of the previous turn. They expect an answer about a policy or a procedure to reflect what they told the application about themselves last month. And they still expect every answer to be grounded in the documents they are allowed to read, with citations. Whether the application is a customer support assistant, a document chat inside a SaaS product, or an internal assistant over firm policies, the expectation is the same.

Meeting that expectation is hard, because the context that would sharpen a search lives outside the knowledge base. A user’s location, role, or product tier was often mentioned in an unrelated conversation weeks ago. To use it, the application has to store every conversation, extract durable facts from it, decide which facts matter for the current question, and inject them into the request. When many people share the application, every one of those steps also has to be isolated per user, and so does every document.

Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, now take over these steps: storing each conversation, extracting facts from it, and bringing the relevant facts into the search. You turn this on by adding a memoryConfiguration to the AgenticRetrieveStream request, which makes AgentCore memory a retrieval source alongside your knowledge base. Within the same call, the service restores the conversation, and the planner decides on its own when a fact about the user would help. It retrieves that fact from long-term memory and uses it to compose the sub-queries it sends to the knowledge base. After generating the answer, the service saves the turn back to memory. The same request carries a userContext, so the knowledge base returns only the documents that the user’s access control lists (ACLs) allow. The integration is opt-in and backward compatible. Your application keeps only what is genuinely yours: authenticating the user and passing who they are.

This post reveals how to build such an assistant for many people who share one knowledge base and one memory resource. Each user sees only the documents they may read, and each user’s memory stays private. The running example is an internal employee assistant for AnyCompany, a fictional organization. Employees sign in with Amazon Cognito and ask questions over HR policies, IT guides, engineering runbooks, and sales plans. We show how to read the user’s identity from the Cognito ID token, how to pass it to AgenticRetrieveStream for document ACLs and for memory, how to design memory namespaces for many users, and how to read the trace to see when the planner used memory. Finally, we make AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) enforce per-user memory isolation even when application code gets it wrong. If you deployed the application from Build multi-tenant agentic chat applications on enterprise data with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, this post replaces its “persist conversation history yourself” step.

It has been revealed that anyCompany keeps its documents in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). One managed knowledge base syncs them through an ACL-enabled Amazon S3 data source. A global ACL file in the same bucket says which employees may read each folder: everyone reads HR and IT, only engineers read the engineering runbooks, and only salespeople read the commission plan. One AgentCore memory resource is shared by every employee. Amazon Cognito authenticates employees, and its ID token supplies two claims: the sub (user ID) identifies the user’s memory, and the verified email identifies the user to the knowledge base’s ACL filter. Three test users sign in: two engineers, Maya and Liam, and one salesperson, Sofia. The trace excerpts in this post are taken from a run of the sample application in the GitHub repository.

It has been revealed that figure 1: Architecture of the memory-aware employee assistant. The application authenticates the user and constructs the request (steps 1–4). Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base restores the session, retrieves information, returns an answer, and saves the exchange to AgentCore memory (steps 5–8). Short-term events and long-term records belong to the same memory resource.

Figure 2: One AgenticRetrieveStream turn with userContext and memoryConfiguration. Everything between the first and last arrow is the service’s work.

In a recent development, managed Knowledge Base owns ingestion, ACL filtering, indexing, ranking, planning, retrieval, and generation. With memoryConfiguration, it also owns session restore, memory search, and persistence. AgentCore memory owns storage, retention, encryption, and extraction. Your application owns authentication, the UI, and reading the user’s identity from the token. There is no conversation table: when the UI lists or reopens a conversation, it reads the same memory resource.

According to recent reports, every value is derived by the application from the verified ID token. None comes from the request body.

Two different claims do two different jobs. The knowledge base identifies users by email, because that is what the connected data source records in its ACLs. Memory needs an actorId that never changes and is never reused. The Cognito sub is both. An email address can be changed, or reassigned to a upcoming employee after someone leaves, and that person would then inherit the old memory. You can use another stable user ID from your own user store as the actorId. What matters is that it never moves to a different person.

The following steps create the knowledge base and its data source, set up the memory resource and Amazon Cognito, build the request, and read the trace to confirm the result.

A managed knowledge base needs no vector store:.

According to recent reports, configure the service role for your setup by following Create a service role for managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, and pass its ARN in roleArn. For model access requirements, also review the prerequisites for managed and custom models.

Industry observers note that documents live in the bucket under docs//. Amazon S3 has no permission system of its own to crawl, so you supply the ACLs in a global ACL file in the same bucket. Each entry maps an S3 prefix to the emails that may read it:.

The sample’s file also gives everyone docs/it/. Then create the data source. For a managed knowledge base, every connector has the type MANAGED_KNOWLEDGE_BASE_CONNECTOR, and connectorParameters.type picks the source:.

In a recent development, aclEnabled cannot be changed after the data source is created. CreateDataSource is asynchronous, so wait for the status AVAILABLE. Then call StartIngestionJob and wait for COMPLETE. The sync reads the documents and the ACL file and indexes each document with its ACL. In the sample, all 11 documents were scanned and indexed with 0 failures. A document that no ACL entry covers is not ingested, and a user whose email matches no entry receives no results from this data source.

It has been revealed that the same model applies to connectors that crawl permissions from the source system, such as Microsoft SharePoint, Google Drive, and Atlassian Confluence. There, the permissions come from the source, groups are resolved from the source, and the knowledge base also checks each result against the source in real time. Your application code does not change: it still passes the user’s email in userContext. For the full list, see Access Control Lists awareness enablement.

One memory resource serves every user. Per-user separation comes from {actorId} in the namespace templates, which AgentCore memory resolves from each event at extraction time. Two choices matter.

Sources indicate that strategies. The two strategies extract different things. The summary strategy summarizes each conversation, so it captures facts that a user mentions in passing, such as “I’m on a Mac in the Frankfurt office.” Those facts are what personalize a later answer about, say, PTO. The user-preference strategy extracts stated preferences into structured records (“Prefers short bullet-point answers without tables”, “Always deploys to eu-central-1 first”) and does not treat incidental mentions as preferences. Summaries give you “what we discussed.” Preferences give you “how this person wants to be answered.” Use both.

Layout. retrievalConfigs accepts one entry, so a single namespacePath must reach everything the planner should see for a user. Put {actorId} directly under the root: namespacePath: "/anycompany/" then covers the profile and every conversation summary. A layout such as /anycompany/profile/{actorId} and /anycompany/summaries/{actorId} would let one entry reach only one of them.

Wait for the memory to reach ACTIVE. Creating the memory does not need a user or actorId, so the order of Step 2 and Step 3 does not matter. Nothing is provisioned per user: a latest Cognito user becomes a new actor the first time they ask a question.

Recent findings suggest that create a user pool and an app client without a client secret. The email decides which documents a user may read, so make it required, verified, and not changeable by the user:.

According to recent reports, mutable cannot be changed after the pool is created. With a mutable email, a signed-in user could change their email to a colleague’s address. If your people federate from Okta or Microsoft Entra ID, map the IdP’s email to this attribute so that it matches the email in your data source’s ACLs.

Sources indicate that the sample enables USER_PASSWORD_AUTH so the local UI and tests can sign in directly. Production applications typically use Cognito managed login or AWS Amplify.

Set up an IAM role for the application. The backend assumes it once per user, with the session tag userId=, and every memory statement is conditioned on that tag. This is the complete policy the sample runs with:.

Recent findings suggest that listEvents is required with sessionBinding, RetrieveMemoryRecords with retrievalConfigs, and CreateEvent when persistenceMode is DEFAULT. ListSessions and ListMemoryRecords are for the application’s own reads (conversation list and the “what memory knows about you” view), not for AgenticRetrieveStream. The role’s trust policy allows sts:AssumeRole, sts:TagSession, and sts:SetSourceIdentity from the backend’s own identity (an AWS Lambda execution role or an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task role in production). If the memory uses a customer managed key, add kms:Decrypt on that key.

Verify the ID token and read the two claims. Only the ID token carries email. The access token does not:.

Recent findings suggest that jwt.decode checks the signature, the issuer (your user pool), the expiry, and the audience (your app client). For details of the claims, see Understanding the identity (ID) token. With API Gateway, a JWT authorizer does the same checks and passes the claims to your handler.

Next, get the user’s AWS credentials. The backend assumes the application role for this user and caches the session until shortly before it expires:.

Every call for this user, including the memory calls that agentic retrieval makes on the caller’s behalf, now runs as assumed-role/anycompany-assistant-app-role/user- and carries the tag that the policy in Step 3 checks.

Decide the sessionId. For a new conversation, the application generates one, such as "conv-" + uuid4().hex, and returns it to the client. To continue a conversation, the client sends it back. To show a user their conversations, call ListSessions with the user’s actorId:.

You do not need your own table that maps consumers to sessions. Accepting a sessionId from the client is safe because short-term memory is keyed by (memoryId, actorId, sessionId), and the actorId comes from the token. If Liam sends Maya’s sessionId, it names a session inside Liam’s own space, which is empty. Agentic retrieval itself does not verify that the actorId, sessionId, or namespace you supply belong to the user who is asking, so they must never come from the client. Keep your own session table only if you need data that memory does not hold, such as conversation titles.

Without userContext, an ACL-enabled data source returns no results at all. Compare the request with the stateless handler it replaces:.

The query before the call and the write after it are gone, and messages has one element. Three rules come with sessionBinding, and each is enforced with a specific ValidationException. First, messages carries only the current question, so you choose one history source per request. Second, persistenceMode: DEFAULT (the default) writes the question and the generated answer as one event, so it requires generateResponse: true. Third, memoryId alone is invalid. persistenceMode: NONE restores history and writes nothing, for audit or replay views.

In a recent development, the client sends { question, sessionId? }. On a newly introduced conversation, the application generates a sessionId and returns it as the first streamed frame. The client echoes it on later turns and omits it to start over.

Because the memory resource is yours, the application reads it directly to render a conversation:.

Each persisted turn is exactly one event with two payloads: the user’s question and the final answer. The history therefore renders as a clean transcript and remains usable by other AgentCore memory clients.

The trace tells you, per turn, what the knowledge base and memory did:.

Sources indicate that the following runs show the behavior. Excerpts are verbatim, trimmed for length.

Document ACLs: Maya and Sofia, same question. “What is the weekly on-call stipend?” The on-call guide is in docs/engineering/. Maya’s retrieval included docs/engineering/oncall.md, and the answer was “500 USD or 450 EUR per week.” Sofia’s speculative retrieval and the planner’s follow-up sub-query returned only HR and sales chunks:.

Recent findings suggest that her answer said that no on-call stipend is documented in the sources she can access. The application made no access decision. It passed userContext.userId: "sofia@example.com", and the knowledge base did the filtering. The reverse holds for the commission plan: Sofia gets the 12% accelerator, and Maya’s retrieval does not contain docs/sales/.

In a recent development, turn 1: Maya, new conversation. “How do I set up the VPN on my laptop? I’m on a Mac in the Frankfurt office.”.

The answer gives the Frankfurt gateway (vpn-fra.anycompany.example) and the macOS steps. Afterwards, ListEvents on the session reveals one event with two payloads.

Turn 2: Maya, same conversation. “It keeps disconnecting every few minutes. What should I try?” The request carried only that sentence:.

In a recent development, the planner sent retrieve("VPN disconnects every few minutes troubleshooting") and retrieve("Cisco Secure Client macOS frequent disconnect fix"). The answer resolved “it” and pointed at iCloud Private Relay, the macOS-specific cause in the guide. On a continued session, SpeculativeRetrieval queries only the knowledge base. The long-term memory lookup in that step happens on upcoming sessions.

Turn 3: Maya, a fresh conversation, later. “How many days of PTO do I get per year, and do unused days carry over?” Her office decides the answer, and she never mentioned it in this conversation. Speculative retrieval searched long-term memory with the raw question and found one record:.

Knowledge base and memory items share one retrievalResponse. Tell them apart by sourceRetriever.identifier or by the _memory_* keys. The record was the summary of her VPN conversation. That was enough: the planner went straight to the answer, which remarked “Since your memory indicates you’re based in the Frankfurt office … you get 30 days of PTO per year, granted in full on January 1, and any unused days must be used by March 31 of the following year.” A fact from an IT conversation personalized an HR answer.

Turn 4: Liam, fresh conversation, identical question. Same handler, same memory resource, a different token. Speculative retrieval found nothing about him, so the planner decided to search memory with its own query:.

Liam received the table of all three offices and a request to say which one he is in. The application chooses where the planner may look. The planner decides whether to look and what to ask: a memoryRetrieve action appears only when the planner decides that another memory search would help. Reading Maya’s sessionId through the history endpoint with Liam’s token returned an empty list.

Figure 3: The same question from two consumers. Maya’s trace demonstrates a memory hit and a Frankfurt-specific answer. Liam’s trace shows zero memory records and the generic table.

It has been revealed that long-term extraction is asynchronous and runs after the turn is persisted. In our run, the first record appeared 81 seconds after turn 2, but the timing is not a commitment. Design for eventual availability. A fact stated in this conversation is not guaranteed to be retrievable in the next one immediately. The sample polls ListMemoryRecords before running turn 3.

In this walkthrough, the application authenticates. The knowledge base filters. ACL-aware retrieval is filtering, not authorization. Take the email only from a verified ID token with email_verified: true, make it immutable in the pool, and handle email reuse: if an address is reassigned to a different person, that person gets the old owner’s document access. The knowledge base fails closed: a document with no ACL, or an ACL error, means fewer results, not extra ones. If results are missing, check that the email matches the ACL entry.

Identity comes from the token (Step 4) for memory too: actorId and namespace come from the verified sub, never from the client.

Recent findings suggest that IAM condition keys, as defense in depth. AgentCore memory exposes bedrock-agentcore:actorId on ListEvents, CreateEvent, and ListSessions, and bedrock-agentcore:namespacePath on RetrieveMemoryRecords and ListMemoryRecords. The memory calls that agentic retrieval makes during a request are authorized against the calling identity. That is why the caller’s policy must grant those actions, and why the conditions in Step 3 apply to them. With the session assumed for Maya, a request bound to Maya’s actorId proceeds normally. A request that binds Liam’s actorId is the bug that this policy guards against, and it is denied at every memory operation:.

It has been revealed that nothing was written to Liam’s memory: his session count stayed at 0. The answer was still generated from the knowledge base. Because each user has their own role session, AWS also sees which user each call is for: the caller is assumed-role/anycompany-assistant-app-role/user- with SourceIdentity=, which the session holder cannot change.

Recent findings suggest that two further points. The memory is a customer-owned resource that other systems in your account may also write to. Treat its contents as input, and attach an Amazon Bedrock guardrail to the request through policyConfiguration. And proposal the data lifecycle. Raw events expire per eventExpiryDuration, but extracted records do not. A user-deletion workflow therefore covers DeleteEvent for the actor’s sessions and DeleteMemoryRecord under the actor’s namespace.

Sources indicate that log the full trace with a correlation ID per turn. The planner’s sub-queries are as worth auditing as its final results. AWS/Bedrock/KnowledgeBases reports Invocations, ClientErrors, and TotalIterationCount for Operation=AgenticRetrieveStream. AWS/Bedrock-AgentCore reports Invocations, Latency, Errors, and UserErrors per memory operation, and InputTokenUsage/OutputTokenUsage per strategy for extraction. With Amazon CloudWatch Transaction Search enabled, AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, reveals a turn’s spans end to end.

According to recent reports, memory operations are best-effort by design. If a memory call fails or is denied, the request does not fail. The trace carries a FAILED memory event with the failure message, and the turn continues without that memory. The answer is generated from the knowledge base. Decide whether your UI surfaces that degraded state.

Run python infra/teardown.py in the sample to delete the knowledge base, the S3 bucket and its objects, the memory resource (including conversation history and long-term records), the Cognito user pool, and the IAM roles.

Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base already gave you the retrieval stack as a service. That stack covers ingestion, document ACLs, indexing, ranking, and the planning loop in AgenticRetrieveStream that turns a hard question into a cited answer. With memoryConfiguration, the same call now carries the conversation and the user’s history. For a multi-user application, that removed the conversation store, the history replay, and the extraction pipeline. What remained was a short list of responsibilities. Authenticate the user and read two claims from the ID token: pass the verified email as userContext so that the knowledge base filters documents, and use the sub as the actorId for one memory resource with {actorId}-rooted namespaces. Use IAM condition keys on a per-user role session as a second line of defense that holds through the agentic path.

Recent findings suggest that to get started, deploy the sample from the GitHub repository. Then read the AgenticRetrieveStream API reference, Access Control Lists awareness enablement, and Use AgentCore memory with agentic retrieval. For the retrieval loop itself, see Agentic retrieval for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base. For memory concepts, see Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory: Building context-aware agents.

#13. XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1179 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1179 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help people who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail.
  • A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y.
  • Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help people who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer people away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

In a recent development, people use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

Sources indicate that for the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

In a recent development, A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:.

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

Recent findings suggest that A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Sources indicate that researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what owners need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench presently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run.
  • Sources indicate that today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's.
  • According to recent reports, the router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Sources indicate that today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

According to recent reports, the router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:.

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent.

In a recent development, the same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise aims include monthly credits for compute and inference.

Industry observers note that on OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

Sources indicate that the best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

It has been revealed that openRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

In a recent development, when a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:.

Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two newly introduced tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics reveals the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:.

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:.

Industry observers note that in your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

Industry observers note that requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

Sources indicate that this is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:.

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.
